title: Freeze-drying kefir grains, sourdough starter, and cultures
description: What is documented about culture survival in freeze-drying — lab lyophilization figures, the one manufacturer claim, and the numbers nobody has published.

faq.question: Does freeze-drying keep a sourdough starter alive?
faq.answer: One manufacturer states that freeze drying retains the culture “without losing its fermentative potential,” publishing no survival figure or measurement [1]. A secondary source states fermentation activity declines within a year even as nutritional value persists [2]. No home-machine survival percentage has been published by anyone, and Sublime Pantry has not tested it.

faq.question: What percentage of cultures survive freeze-drying?
faq.answer: In laboratory studies, L. rhamnosus GG survived at about 12% when dried in water alone and 15.17% ± 4.43 in trehalose plus skim milk [5]; a yeast starter survived at 0.01–0.27% with no protective agent and 94.2–97% in a skim milk, maltose and maltitol blend [6]. These are lab lyophilization figures, not home freeze dryer figures.

faq.question: Are there published numbers for kefir grains?
faq.answer: Three peer-reviewed studies address freeze-dried kefir grains directly [7][8][9]. We confirmed they exist and are on topic, but could not retrieve their figures — the papers returned paywalls, 403 responses, and CAPTCHA challenges. No number from them appears in this article.

faq.question: Do I need a cryoprotectant at home?
faq.answer: The lab record shows protective agents moving yeast survival from 0.01–0.27% to 94.2–97% [6], and changing L. rhamnosus GG survival as well [5]. No manufacturer or extension source addresses cryoprotection for home freeze-drying, so there is no published home practice to follow — that absence is the finding.

faq.question: How should freeze-dried cultures be stored?
faq.answer: No source publishes storage temperature, humidity, or packaging conditions specific to home freeze-dried cultures [1][2]. General storage guidance for freeze-dried food is mylar plus an oxygen absorber, kept cool, dark, dry and below 85°F [13]; extension services dispute the 25-year claim attached to it and recommend 5–10 years for home-produced food [10][11].

howTo.name: Dry the starter at its most active
howTo.text: Freeze-dry the starter while it is lively and bubbling, spread thinly on parchment [1]. No source specifies a thickness or a drying temperature for cultures.

howTo.name: Pre-freeze and load
howTo.text: Pre-freeze the trays overnight and fill them about three-quarters full; the published cycle estimate is roughly 24 hours [2, secondary].

howTo.name: Confirm the tray has stopped losing weight
howTo.text: Weigh the tray at cycle completion and again after any extended dry time, allowing about a 1 g scale error; consistent weight indicates the food is adequately dry [12].

howTo.name: Rehydrate with filtered water
howTo.text: Revive with warm filtered water rather than tap water, because chlorine may hinder yeast recovery [1].

bodyHtml:
The short version: Every survival percentage published for freeze-dried cultures comes from laboratory lyophilization, not from a home machine — Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG fell to about 12% survival when dried in water alone, and a yeast starter dried without protective agents survived at 0.01–0.27% [5][6]. One home-machine manufacturer states that freeze drying keeps a sourdough starter's fermentative potential, without publishing a survival figure, a measurement method, or a cryoprotectant [1]. No source compares a home unit's results to the lab record, so what a kitchen freeze dryer does to a live culture is undocumented rather than settled.

What the peer-reviewed record actually measures

The clearest number in the literature is the gap between freezing and drying. Freezing and thawing L. rhamnosus GG in liquid nitrogen left 90.94% ± 12.82 of cells viable; putting the same organism through a full freeze-drying cycle in water as the sole medium left roughly 12% [5]. The damage the studies measure is mostly in the drying, not the freezing.

The second number is what protective agents do. A yeast starter dried with no protective agent survived at 0.01–0.27%; the same strain dried in a skim milk, maltose and maltitol blend survived at 94.2–97% immediately after drying, and 61% after 42 weeks of refrigerated storage [6].

OrganismConditionSurvivalSource
L. rhamnosus GGFreeze–thaw only, liquid nitrogen −196 °C, 2 h90.94% ± 12.82[5]
L. rhamnosus GGFreeze–thaw only, −80 °C, 2 h77.19% ± 13.30[5]
L. rhamnosus GGFreeze–thaw only, −40 °C, 2 h77.68% ± 3.29[5]
L. rhamnosus GGFull freeze-drying, water as sole medium~12%[5]
L. rhamnosus GGFull freeze-drying, PBS~2%[5]

S. cerevisiae 88-4No protective agents0.01–0.27%[6]
S. cerevisiae 88-4Skim milk + maltose + maltitol, immediately after drying94.2–97%[6]
S. cerevisiae 88-4Same blend, after 42 weeks refrigerated61%[6]

Read the table as a range, not a forecast. These are single strains, in named media, under laboratory freezing and vacuum control. They tell you what the process can do to a culture; they do not tell you what your machine did to yours.

What a home unit does not provide

No source we could retrieve compares a home freeze dryer to a laboratory lyophilizer for culture survival. The comparison is absent in both directions — nobody publishes that home units match lab results, and nobody publishes that they fall short.

What is visible is a difference in method, stated here as an observation about equipment rather than a claim about outcome. The studies above use programmable freezing ramps, liquid nitrogen or −80 °C ultra-freezers, and cryoprotectant blends formulated to a specified percentage [5][6]. A consumer machine offers a single freeze stage, a fixed vacuum, and no formulation step. Whether that difference costs one order of magnitude in viability or none is exactly the number nobody has published.

Sourdough starter: one manufacturer claim, one source that disagrees

The only manufacturer statement we located is Stay Fresh: “A unique preservation technology, freeze drying, retains this live culture without losing its fermentative potential” [1]. That page publishes no survival percentage, no measurement method, and no mention of cryoprotection anywhere.

A secondary source disagrees on duration: it describes freeze-dried starter as shelf stable for 20–25 years and holding 90–95% of nutritional value, while stating that bacterial and fermentation activity declines within one year if the starter is meant to be revived as an active culture, and recommending annual replacement [2]. Neither side addresses the other, and neither publishes a measurement. Both positions are recorded here as published; we have not reconciled them and have not tested either.

The preparation steps that are published

  • Dry the starter while it is “lively, bubbling,” spread thinly on parchment [1].
  • Pre-freeze trays overnight and fill them about three-quarters full; the cycle is described as roughly 24 hours [2, secondary].
  • Rehydrate with warm filtered water: tap water's chlorine “may hinder yeast recovery” [1].

That is the whole published procedure. No source specifies a drying temperature for cultures, a target residual moisture, a cryoprotectant, or a way to check that the culture is alive short of trying to feed it.

Kefir grains: three studies exist, and the numbers are behind walls

Three peer-reviewed studies address freeze-dried kefir directly: a Journal of Dairy Research paper on viability and probiotic properties of a kefir-derived bacteria-and-yeast mixture [7], Kök Tas on storage parameters for freeze-dried kefir grains [8], and a Processes paper on Mexican kefir grains [9]. We confirmed all three exist and match the topic. We could not retrieve their survival figures — the attempts returned paywalls, 403s, and CAPTCHA challenges.

So the honest state of kefir grains here is: the research has been done, it is on point, and this article cannot tell you what it found. Anyone publishing a kefir-grain survival percentage without institutional access to those papers is not getting it from them.

Drying a culture does not make anything safe

The same mechanism that keeps a starter alive keeps everything else alive. Utah State University Extension's Jose Brandao: “Freeze-drying does not kill bacteria. Instead, it preserves microorganisms in a dormant state” [3]. Dormant organisms reactivate when water is added back [3][4]. That is the appeal of the process for a culture and the reason it changes nothing about the safety of the milk, flour, or water the culture lives in.

Storage: what is claimed and what extension services say

Harvest Right states that properly packaged freeze-dried food “can last up to 25 years or longer under ideal conditions” in mylar with an oxygen absorber, kept cool, dark, dry and below 85 °F [13]. Three extension sources push back on the figure for home-produced food: Utah State University states that “no real data exists on the shelf-life of home freeze-dried products,” noting the first home unit went on sale in 2013 [10], and UC ANR states the claim “has not been corroborated by university studies for home freeze dryers,” recommending consumption within 5–10 years [11].

For cultures the record is thinner still. No source we found publishes storage temperature, humidity, or packaging conditions for a home freeze-dried starter [1][2] — and the one long-term storage figure in the peer-reviewed record moves in the other direction, with yeast viability falling from 94.2–97% to 61% over 42 weeks in refrigerated storage, in a formulated protective medium [6].

On the dryness endpoint, Stay Fresh publishes the most specific method we located: weigh the tray at cycle completion and again after extended drying, allowing about a 1 g scale error, and treat consistent weight as adequately dry [12]. Packaging for long-term storage is mylar plus an oxygen absorber in the sources above [13]; our Freeze-Drying Packaging Starter Kit (100 mylar bags in three sizes, 100 absorbers, labels) is one way to buy that combination — Sold by Sublime Pantry.

What we could not source

  • Kefir grain survival percentages. Three on-topic peer-reviewed studies identified [7][8][9]; all three unretrievable across repeated attempts (paywall, 403, CAPTCHA). Titles and existence confirmed; no figures obtained.
  • Yogurt culture viability after home freeze-drying. A relevant paper on probiotic survival in freeze-dried yogurt starter cultures was identified but not fetched or verified. No manufacturer viability claim for yogurt cultures was verified.
  • Any home-versus-lab comparison. Searched directly for whether home units can reproduce lab lyophilization survival rates. No source makes the comparison in either direction.
  • Extension guidance on cultures. No extension service publishes freeze-drying guidance specific to sourdough starter, kefir grains, or yogurt cultures. The National Center for Home Food Preservation publishes no home freeze-drying guidance at all — its freezing and drying pages cover conventional methods, and its freeze-drying educator page is subscriber-gated.
  • A residual-moisture target. Every moisture figure in the category is framed as percent removed, never percent remaining — for cultures or for anything else.
  • A cryoprotectant practice for home use. The lab record shows protective agents changing survival by orders of magnitude [5][6]; no manufacturer or extension source mentions cryoprotection for home freeze-drying at all.
